subject: Legal Studies
name: Legal Studies, Units 1 and 2
syllabus: VCE Legal Studies Study Design (from 2024), Units 1 and 2

points.title: Laws and social cohesion
points.brief: Individuals, laws and the legal system work together to keep society stable and protect each person's rights.

points.title: Principles of justice
points.brief: Justice rests on fairness (fair processes), equality (the same treatment, or different treatment where needed) and access (understanding the system and using it).

points.title: Characteristics of an effective law
points.brief: An effective law reflects society's values, is enforceable, is known, is clear and is stable.

points.title: Parliament and the courts
points.brief: Parliament makes most laws. Courts apply them and make law through precedent and statutory interpretation.

points.title: Sources of law
points.brief: Law comes from parliament (statute law) and from judges' decisions in cases (common law).

points.title: The Victorian court hierarchy
points.brief: Courts are ranked from the Magistrates' Court through the County Court to the Supreme Court, so cases go to courts suited to them and decisions can be appealed.

points.title: Criminal and civil law
points.brief: Criminal law deals with offences against society, brought by the state. Civil law deals with disputes between people. One act, such as an assault, can lead to both.

points.title: Purposes of criminal law
points.brief: Criminal law protects people and property, sets standards of behaviour and allows punishment of those who break them.

points.title: The presumption of innocence
points.brief: An accused person is treated as innocent until proven guilty, and has the right to silence.

points.title: Burden and standard of proof in criminal cases
points.brief: The prosecution must prove the accused guilty beyond reasonable doubt.

points.title: Elements of a crime
points.brief: Most crimes need a guilty act (actus reus) and a guilty mind (mens rea), proven together.

points.title: Strict liability offences
points.brief: Offences such as many traffic offences need only the act proven, with no need to show intent.

points.title: Age of criminal responsibility
points.brief: Below a set age a child cannot be charged with a crime. Above it, up to 14, the prosecution must show the child knew it was seriously wrong.

points.title: Summary and indictable offences
points.brief: Summary offences are minor and heard in the Magistrates' Court. Indictable offences are serious and can be tried before a judge and jury.

points.title: Participants in a crime
points.brief: Principal offenders commit the crime. Accessories help them after it, and people can also be charged for helping before or during it.

points.title: An offence against the person
points.brief: Offences such as assault and homicide harm a person's body or life, and each has elements the prosecution must prove.

points.title: An offence against property
points.brief: Offences such as theft and burglary take or damage property, and each has elements the prosecution must prove.

points.title: Defences
points.brief: A defence such as self-defence or duress, if accepted, can mean the accused is not guilty or is guilty of a lesser offence.

points.title: Trends and impact of an offence
points.brief: Crime statistics show how often an offence happens in Victoria and elsewhere, and its harm reaches victims, families and the wider community.

points.title: Police and enforcement bodies
points.brief: Victoria Police and bodies given powers by law, such as transport officers, investigate and enforce criminal law.

points.title: Police powers and individual rights
points.brief: Powers to arrest, search and question are balanced by rights such as the right to silence and to a lawyer.

points.title: Courts in criminal cases
points.brief: The Magistrates' Court hears summary offences, the County Court most indictable ones, and the Supreme Court the most serious, such as murder.

points.title: The jury in a criminal trial
points.brief: Twelve people from the community decide the facts and whether the accused is guilty beyond reasonable doubt.

points.title: Groups facing difficulties
points.brief: First Nations people, young people, people from other cultures and languages, and people with mental illness or disability can face extra barriers in the criminal system.

points.title: Purposes of sanctions
points.brief: Sanctions aim to punish, deter the offender and others, denounce the crime, protect the community and rehabilitate the offender.

points.title: Fines
points.brief: A sum of money paid to the state, set by the offence and the offender's ability to pay.

points.title: Community correction orders
points.brief: A sanction served in the community, with conditions such as unpaid work, treatment or supervision.

points.title: Imprisonment
points.brief: The most serious sanction, used as a last resort, which removes the offender from the community.

points.title: Factors in sentencing
points.brief: Judges weigh aggravating factors, such as violence, and mitigating factors, such as a guilty plea or remorse.

points.title: Alternative approaches to sentencing
points.brief: The Drug Court, the Koori Court and diversion programs try to deal with the causes of offending and reduce reoffending.

points.title: Sentencing in another state
points.brief: Comparing how another Australian jurisdiction sentences offenders shows other ways to meet the same purposes.

points.title: Purposes of civil law
points.brief: Civil law protects rights and lets a wronged party be put back where they were. Its areas include negligence, defamation, contract and nuisance.

points.title: Breach, causation and loss
points.brief: A civil claim needs a breach of the law, proof that the breach caused the harm, and a loss such as injury, damage or lost income.

points.title: Burden and standard of proof in civil cases
points.brief: The plaintiff must prove their case on the balance of probabilities.

points.title: Parties to a civil dispute
points.brief: The plaintiff brings the claim and the defendant answers it. A group of plaintiffs can bring a class action.

points.title: Limitation of actions
points.brief: A civil claim must be brought within a set time, such as six years for many claims, or it can be lost.

points.title: Negligence
points.brief: A defendant is liable in negligence if they owed a duty of care, breached it, and caused harm that was not too remote.

points.title: Defences to negligence
points.brief: Contributory negligence reduces damages. Voluntary assumption of risk can defeat the claim.

points.title: Defamation
points.brief: Publishing something that harms a person's reputation can be defamation. Defences include truth and honest opinion, and damages are the usual remedy.

points.title: The impact of a civil wrong
points.brief: A breach can cost the injured party money, health and reputation, and can cost the defendant money and standing too.

points.title: Justice in civil disputes
points.brief: Fairness, equality and access apply to civil disputes too: a fair process, equal treatment and the ability to use the system.

points.title: Ways of settling civil disputes
points.brief: Negotiation, mediation, conciliation and arbitration settle disputes without a full trial.

points.title: Bodies that settle disputes
points.brief: Tribunals such as VCAT, ombudsmen and complaints bodies such as Consumer Affairs Victoria settle many disputes without a court.

points.title: Courts in civil disputes
points.brief: The Magistrates' Court hears smaller claims, the County Court larger ones, and the Supreme Court the largest and most complex.

points.title: The jury in a civil trial
points.brief: In some civil trials, six jurors decide the facts, whether the defendant is liable and sometimes the damages.

points.title: Groups facing difficulties in civil justice
points.brief: First Nations people, people on low incomes, young people and people in rural and remote areas can find civil justice hard to reach.

points.title: Purposes of remedies
points.brief: A remedy aims to restore the plaintiff to their position before the wrong, or stop the wrong continuing.

points.title: Compensatory damages
points.brief: Money to make up for loss, covering financial losses and pain and suffering.

points.title: Other kinds of damages
points.brief: Nominal damages recognise a wrong with a small sum, contemptuous damages show the court thought little of the claim, and exemplary damages punish.

points.title: Injunctions
points.brief: A court order to stop doing something (restrictive) or to do something (mandatory).

points.title: What human rights are
points.brief: Basic rights and freedoms every person has, which grew out of history and were set out in 1948 in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

points.title: Rights in the Constitution
points.brief: The Australian Constitution protects a few rights expressly, such as freedom of religion, and the High Court has found implied rights, such as political communication.

points.title: Rights in statute and common law
points.brief: Parliaments protect rights through laws such as anti-discrimination acts, and courts protect them through common law.

points.title: The Victorian Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities
points.brief: A Victorian statute that lists rights, requires laws to be read consistently with them, and requires public authorities to consider them.

points.title: International treaties and Australia
points.brief: Australia has signed human rights treaties, but they bind locally only when parliament makes them part of Australian law.

points.title: Studying a human rights issue
points.brief: Students study one right in Australia, how it developed and which laws protect it, such as freedom of expression or the right to vote.

points.title: Conflicting attitudes to a right
points.brief: People and groups often disagree on how far a right should go and how it should be balanced against others.

points.title: Reforming rights protection
points.brief: Changes to protect a right better can come through new laws, a charter of rights or the courts.

points.title: People who changed rights
points.brief: Individuals and groups have pushed governments and courts to protect rights better, through cases, campaigns and protest.
